title: Ethics as practice
hook: the second perfection: keep your precepts as a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving as practice: rice into a bowl, and even the last mouthful shared. Your line was the first perfection. What did you give before you ate? Day one thousand four hundred.

A rule is usually something you keep for your own sake, or to stay out of trouble. Don't speed, and you won't get a ticket. Don't lie, and you won't get caught. Now turn that around. What if every rule you kept were a present you handed to someone else? Not to the police, not to a teacher, but to the stranger on the sidewalk, the person in the next apartment, the animal in the yard. That's the startling turn the Buddha gives to ethics. Yesterday the perfections began with giving. Today the second one, ethics, turns out to be giving too, only quieter. Today: ethics as practice.
screen: `A RULE KEPT FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.` → `TURN IT AROUND.` → `A PRESENT TO A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali it is sila: ethics, good conduct, the way you live with others. It comes second in both lists of perfections, right after giving. For lay Buddhists, it is shaped by the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind. Second, the surprise. In a discourse in the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha calls these precepts five gifts. When someone keeps the first, not to kill, they give beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from harm. And the text says this gift reaches beings without limit, and that the giver shares in the same freedom. Nobody near you has to wonder whether you will hurt them. That is a gift, even if no one ever knows you gave it. Third, the heart of the teaching. A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, sums it up: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the order. Stop harming first. Then do good. Then the mind. Ethics is the ground the rest stands on. Fourth, keeping them again. The precepts are not vows taken once and forgotten. In temples and homes, they are recited again and taken up afresh. A slip is not the end. It is a reason to begin again tomorrow. This week the path walked to Sarnath, Kushinagar and Vulture Peak, around an island and a mountain, and then turned to the perfections. The road turns out to be under your own feet.
screen: `SILA, THE SECOND PERFECTION.` · `FIVE PRECEPTS, FIVE GIFTS.` · `STOP HARM, DO GOOD, CLEAR THE MIND.` · then, large: `FREEDOM FROM FEAR.`

segments.voice: For this sit, if you'd like, let the breath settle first. Then choose one precept for today, whichever one speaks to you: not harming, not taking, honest speech, care with your body, or a clear mind. Say it quietly in your own words, as something you intend for one day. Then bring to mind the people and creatures you'll pass today, and let them be the ones receiving it. They will never know. It is still a gift. Rest with that for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Ethics as practice. Sila, the second perfection: keeping the precepts carefully, as a gift of safety and freedom from fear to everyone around you. Today's word.
Your line: the second perfection. Today, keep your one precept carefully, and each time you keep it, remember who received the gift. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take or renew the five precepts by reciting them in Pali or in their own language, at the temple or at home, and some keep additional precepts on observance days.

fork.setup: you keep the precept not to kill, and no one ever notices. by the Buddha's words, what have you done?
fork.reveal: in the Numerical Discourses he calls it a gift: freedom from fear, hostility and harm, given to beings without limit, and shared by the giver.

original.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): ethics, good conduct, the second perfection.

trapdoor: what you thought: ethics is a list of rules.
what it means: a practice of not harming, kept carefully and renewed, that others receive as safety.
what a scholar hears: sila as the second perfection, the five precepts called five great gifts in the Numerical Discourses, and Dhammapada 183's order: stop harm, do good, purify the mind.

sources.quoted: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.

notes: Dhammapada 183 quoted from Max Müller (SBE X, 1881), including his parenthesis '(all)'; confirm exact wording.

AN 8.39 paraphrased: abstaining from killing etc. are 'five gifts' (great gifts) by which one gives freedom from fear, hostility and oppression to limitless beings and gains a share in the same. Confirm.
'It comes second in both lists of perfections': sila is second in the ten paramis and the six paramitas; confirm.
'In temples and homes, they are recited again': recitation of the five precepts at temple services and observance days; confirm or soften to 'some'.
Hook uses everyday examples (speeding ticket) for contrast; the turn is attributed to the Buddha via AN 8.39.
Week end (days 1394–1400): the teach closes by looking back over the week's pilgrimage days and the start of the perfections.
